text_blocks.snippet: Periodontal disease, also known as gum disease, has several risk factors, with the most significant being poor oral hygiene, smoking, and diabetes. Other factors include age, genetics, certain medications, stress, and hormonal changes, especially during pregnancy.
snippet_highlighted_words: poor oral hygiene, smoking, and diabetes

list.title: Poor Oral Hygiene:
list.snippet: Plaque and tartar buildup can irritate gums and lead to inflammation, a key factor in periodontal disease.

list.title: Smoking:
list.snippet: Smoking is a major risk factor, significantly increasing the risk of developing and worsening gum disease.

list.title: Diabetes:
list.snippet: Uncontrolled diabetes impairs the body's ability to fight infection and heal, making individuals more susceptible to gum disease.

list.title: Stress:
list.snippet: Emotional stress can weaken the immune system, making it harder to fight off infections like gum disease.

list.title: Diet:
list.snippet: Poor nutrition, including low intake of vitamins and minerals, can negatively affect oral health and increase the risk of gum disease.

list.title: Medications:
list.snippet: Certain medications can cause dry mouth or other oral side effects that can contribute to gum disease.

list.title: Age:
list.snippet: The risk of periodontal disease increases with age.

list.title: Genetics:
list.snippet: Some individuals may have a genetic predisposition to gum disease, meaning they are more susceptible to the disease even with good oral hygiene.

list.title: Hormonal Changes:
list.snippet: Fluctuations in hormones, such as those during pregnancy or menopause, can increase the risk of gum disease.

list.title: Certain Systemic Diseases:
list.snippet: Conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn's disease, and HIV/AIDS can increase the risk of periodontal disease.
